sections.h2: What kind of county is Kane County, Illinois, for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Kane County is a collar county west of Chicago, with Geneva as the county seat and Aurora as its largest city. It was formed in 1836 out of LaSalle County and covers about 524 square miles, and its biggest cities (Aurora, Elgin, Batavia, St. Charles and Geneva) sit along the Fox River. The county is part of the Chicago metropolitan area, and the 2020 census counted 516,522 residents, which makes it the fifth most populous county in Illinois.

The county is a patchwork of cities, villages and townships, and that matters for a seller because the tax bill for one Kane County house can look very different from the bill for a house a few miles away. Elgin, Aurora, Batavia, Geneva, St. Charles, Carpentersville, Sugar Grove, Montgomery and Hampshire all have their own taxing bodies layered under the county. A Geneva address and a Hampshire address can pay to different school districts, park districts and fire districts, even though both are billed by the same county treasurer.

sections.h2: Which Kane County offices deal with property tax?
sections.html:
Four offices share the work in Kane County, and the Government Center campus in Geneva houses most of them. The county's own quick guide to property taxes sorts questions by office, so a seller can go straight to the right desk.

Kane County property tax offices (source: Kane County Quick Guide to Property Taxes, April 2025)
OfficeHandlesWhere and phone
Township Assessor (16 townships)Initial valuations, questions about your assessed valueDirectory at assessments.kanecountyil.gov
County Assessment OfficeExemptions, assessment complaints, equalization factors719 Batavia Avenue, Building C, Geneva, (630) 208-3818

County TreasurerCurrent tax bills and collection, forfeitures719 Batavia Avenue, Building A, Geneva, (630) 232-3565

The same guide says offices take calls from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays and close on county holidays. Foreclosures go through the county sheriff, a point worth knowing if a sale is racing a lender.

sections.h2: How does Kane County assess a house?
sections.html:
A Kane County township assessor estimates the fair cash value of a home as of January 1 of the assessment year, and the assessed value is 33.33 percent of that figure. Assessors look at actual sales from the three prior years, and the county Supervisor of Assessments then equalizes values so townships line up with each other.

Kane County has 16 townships, and each one elects its own assessor: Aurora, Batavia, Big Rock, Blackberry, Campton, Dundee, Elgin, Geneva, Hampshire, Kaneville, Plato, Rutland, St. Charles, Sugar Grove, Virgil and Burlington. The valuation work happens at the township level, not at the county seat. Between general assessment years, assessors can still revise values for new construction, demolition, or damage from fire or flood.

  • Farmland is valued on agricultural economic value, so a Kane County farm and a southern Illinois farm are valued the same way.
  • Preferential assessments exist for subdivision lots, historic residences, open space, low-income housing, veterans and fraternal posts, solar energy and railroads, each with its own conditions.
  • The county publishes that the tax cap law (PTELL) limits most local levy increases to 5 percent or inflation, whichever is less, with exceptions such as new construction and voter-approved referenda.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Kane County assessment?
sections.html:
Talk to your township assessor first, then file a written complaint with the Kane County Board of Review within 30 days after your township's assessment notice is published in a local newspaper. The Board of Review is a three-member body that can raise, lower or confirm an assessment, and it also decides exemption requests.

Kane County recognizes three bases for a complaint. One is a physical data error, such as a record showing 2,400 square feet when a survey shows 2,200. Another is valuation, where the equalized assessed value is more than one third of fair cash value. The third is equity, where the assessment is higher than comparable homes nearby. The Property Tax Appeal Board has ruled that the dollar amount of the tax or the year-over-year percentage change is not a valid basis for an appeal.

Deadlines vary by township, and the county lists them on its Assessment Complaints page along with residential, commercial and association complaint forms and an electronic evidence portal. Once a tax bill arrives it is too late to complain for that year unless the complaint was already taken to the Board of Review. Subscribing to the assessment office's email notice tells you when your township's roll is published.

sections.h2: Which homestead exemptions does Kane County list?
sections.html:
The county's quick guide lists nine relief programs, and most reduce the taxable value rather than the bill itself. Applications are on the assessment office website or by phone at (630) 208-3818.

  • General Homestead Exemption, up to $8,000, for owner-occupied principal dwellings, usually without annual reapplication.
  • Senior Citizen Homestead Exemption, up to $8,000, for owners 65 or older by December 31 of the assessment year.
  • Homestead Improvement Exemption, up to $25,000, on a new addition or finished basement for four years.
  • Low-Income Senior Citizen Assessment Freeze, with an annual application and a household income limit of $65,000 in the guide.
  • Returning Veterans' Exemption of $5,000 for two years after return from an armed conflict.
  • Standard Exemption for Veterans with Disabilities, up to $250,000, for a service-connected rating of at least 30 percent.
  • Veterans with Disabilities Exemption, up to $100,000, for Specially Adapted Housing.
  • Persons with Disabilities Exemption of $2,000.
  • Natural Disaster Exemption for reconstruction after a disaster.

Senior help is available through Senior Services of Aurora and Senior Services of Elgin, which the guide lists with phone numbers.

sections.h2: When are Kane County property taxes due?
sections.html:
Kane County bills in two installments, and the 2025 taxes payable in 2026 were due June 1 and September 1, 2026. Bills were mailed on or before May 1, and the payment season for that tax year closed on Friday, October 23, 2026 at 4:30 p.m.

State law (35 ILCS 200/21-15) makes an unpaid installment delinquent after its due date and charges interest at 1 1/2 percent per month or portion of a month in counties of this size. Unpaid taxes can be offered at the annual tax sale. The county explains that a buyer of a principal dwelling's taxes leaves the owner a redemption period of two and one half years, and other property gets two years, with costs and interest added to the tax owed. Sold taxes are redeemed through the County Clerk's Tax Extension office, not the treasurer.

Payment options listed by the treasurer include online e-check (free), a drive-up drop box behind Building A, participating Kane County banks with a payment coupon, mail, the treasurer's counter, and the County Clerk's Aurora and Elgin branch offices for personal checks or money orders. A bill reprint is free online or $2.00 at the counter.

sections.h2: Who pays the tax when a Kane County house sells?
sections.html:
The tax follows the property, not the person who owned it, so a Kane County buyer can receive a bill for a year in which the seller lived there. The county tells new owners to read the closing statement for a credit from the seller or to ask their attorney.

Because Illinois taxes are paid in arrears, the bill due in a given year covers the prior year. At a closing, the title company usually prorates the unpaid portion, and the numbers rely on the most recent bill or an estimate. Ask the Kane County Treasurer for the payment status of your parcel number (PIN) and ask the Clerk for an estimate of redemption if a prior year went unpaid. A PIN appears on the bill and on the assessment notice, and the assessment office's Property Search tool will find it by address.

sections.h2: Where does Kane County property tax money go?
sections.html:
The largest share goes to schools, and the rest is split among municipalities, the county and other local governments. Kane County has no say in what other governments levy, since each taxing body sets its own levy and the county issues a levy only for itself.

By property type, the county reports that residential property supplies 75.7 percent of the tax base, commercial 12.8 percent, industrial 9.6 percent and farm 1.7 percent. The county's own extension rose from $58,345,127 for 2023 to $61,071,789 for 2024, an increase of 4.69 percent. Among school districts, the quick guide shows taxes billed for 2024 changing by 5.96 percent in Elgin 46, 3.10 percent in Geneva 304, 5.37 percent in Saint Charles 303 and a drop of 1.62 percent in Batavia 101. The guide gives tax rates generally between about 6 and 9 percent, with a median near 7.5 percent. A parcel lookup at the county's tax data site shows how much goes to each district for one property.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about Kane County homes?
sections.html:
Census QuickFacts lists 525,757 residents for July 2025 and 195,957 housing units. Among Kane County households, 76.0 percent own the home they live in, and the median value of an owner-occupied home for 2020 to 2024 is $327,000. Median gross rent is $1,453, median household income is $103,163, and the average commute is 27.8 minutes.

Median owner costs are $2,256 a month with a mortgage and $958 without one, which shows how much of a Kane County owner's budget a tax bill and insurance can take. Building permits issued in 2025 totaled 1,629. A seller facing back taxes, a delinquent notice or a rental with a tenant should start with the treasurer and the clerk's tax extension office, then decide how to price and time a sale.

faqs.q: Who bills property tax in Kane County, Illinois?
faqs.a: The Kane County Treasurer bills and collects current taxes from Building A of the Government Center in Geneva, phone (630) 232-3565. Tax rates and redemption questions go to the County Clerk's Tax Extension office at (630) 232-5964.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Kane County assessment?
faqs.a: The deadline is 30 days after your township's assessment notice is published in a local newspaper. File with the Board of Review, and check the county's Deadlines page because publication dates differ by township.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay Kane County property tax?
faqs.a: Unpaid installments accrue interest at 1 1/2 percent per month, and the taxes can be offered at the annual tax sale. The owner of a principal dwelling keeps a redemption period of two and one half years, according to the county's guide.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Kane County house with taxes still unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes, but the unpaid amount must be settled at closing or credited to the buyer, because the tax stays with the property. Ask the treasurer for the payoff and the clerk for a redemption estimate if taxes were sold.

faqs.q: Does Kane County offer a senior exemption?
faqs.a: Yes. The Senior Citizen Homestead Exemption is listed at up to $8,000 for owners who are 65 by December 31 of the assessment year, and a separate assessment freeze applies when household income is within the limit shown in the county guide.
